overview: This is a First Amended Complaint filed by Crocs, Inc. on October 22, 2021, in ITC Investigation 337-TA-1270. Crocs alleges that numerous respondents have unlawfully imported and sold casual footwear products that infringe Crocs' federally registered trademark rights in three trademarks: two 3D design marks (U.S. Registration Nos. 5,149,328 and 5,273,875) and one word mark "CROCS" (U.S. Registration No. 3,836,415). The complaint seeks a General Exclusion Order, cease-and-desist orders, and other relief.

points.point: Complainant is Crocs, Inc., a Delaware corporation headquartered in Broomfield, Colorado. Crocs manufactures, sells, and distributes footwear bearing its registered trademarks through numerous retail channels and online platforms worldwide.
points.quote: Crocs, Inc. ("Crocs" or "Complainant"), requests that the United States International Trade Commission ("Commission" or "ITC") institute an investigation under Section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as Amended, 19 U.S.C. § 1337 ("Section 337"), based on the unlawful importation

(China), Bijora, Inc. d/b/a Akira (Illinois), Dr. Leonard's Healthcare Corp. a/k/a Carol Wright (New Jersey), Orly Shoe Corp. (New York), Donggong Eastar Footwear Enterprises Co., Ltd. (Oklahoma), La Modish Boutique (California), Legend Footwear d/b/a Wild Diva (California), Loeffler Randall Inc. (New York), Maxhouse Rise Ltd. (Hong Kong), and others.

(China).
points.quote: PW Shoes, Inc. a/k/a P&W ("PW"); SG Footwear Meser Grp. Inc. a/k/a S. Goldberg & Co. ("SG Footwear"); Shoe-Nami, Inc. ("Shoe-Nami"); Skechers USA, Inc. ("Skechers"); Star Bay Group Inc. ("Star Bay"); Yoki Fashion International LLC ("Yoki")

points.point: The Crocs 3D Marks consist of a three-dimensional shoe design featuring round holes placed across the horizontal portion of the upper and a textured strip along the vertical portion with trapezoidal openings. The '875 Registration also includes a textured strip on the heel and a decorative band along the heel strap.
points.quote: The Crocs 3D Marks both consist of a three-dimensional configuration of the outside of an upper for a shoe, featuring round holes placed across the horizontal portion of the upper, and a textured strip along the vertical portion of the upper having trapezoidal openings.

points.point: Complainant asserts U.S. Trademark Registration No. 5,149,328 (3D Mark), U.S. Trademark Registration No. 5,273,875 (3D Mark with textured heel and decorative band), and U.S. Trademark Registration No. 3,836,415 (CROCS word mark). The 3D Marks were first used in commerce in June 2003 and federally registered on February 28, 2017 and August 29, 2017. The word mark was first used in November 2002 and registered August 24, 2010.
points.quote: Crocs' registered trademarks at issue in the proposed investigation are collectively referred to as the "Asserted Trademarks." Pursuant to Commission Rules 210.10(b)(1) and 210.12(a)(12), Complainant states that a plain English description of the category of Accused Products is casual footwear with holes in the upper and such footwear's packaging.

points.point: The accused products are casual footwear with holes in the upper and packaging thereof. Crocs Shoes are footwear products manufactured and designed by Crocs in the United States, including the Classic Clog and numerous variations thereof sold through major retailers and online platforms, featuring the Asserted Trademarks.
points.quote: Today, Crocs footwear can be found in hundreds of forms and color patterns, ranging from khaki canvas loafers to tie-dyed sandals. Among this wide variety of options, the Classic Clog that features the Crocs 3D Marks, as well as the Crocs Word Mark, remains the company's flagship shoe.

points.point: Representative accused products include Cape Robbin's 'Vigilante' and 'Gardener' footwear; Akira's 'Cape Robbin Electric Soul Flatform Clogs'; La Modish's 'Brandy Slides' and 'Lindsey Crocs'; Dr. Leonard's 'Casual Slingback Clog'; Fullbeauty's 'Kingsize Wide Width Clogs'; and similar clog-style shoes sold by other respondents.
points.quote: Cape Robbin and use a variety of lengthy, descriptive names to market and sell their Accused Products. For example, one type of Accused Product, the "Vigilante" footwear product is sold at least under the following names: "Vigilante-3 Ankle Strap Cut Out Hole Sandal with Pins-Sage", "Vigilante-6 Ankle Strap Cut Out Hole Sandal with Gems-Black"

points.point: The accused products are manufactured abroad (in China, Brazil, and other countries) and are imported into the United States. The products bear labels stating 'Made in China' and are distributed through retailers and e-commerce platforms including Amazon, eBay, and respondents' own websites.
points.quote: The Accused Products are manufactured abroad and are imported into the United States. Specifically, and as seen in the pictures above, the shoes have a label stating "Made in China."

points.point: Crocs alleges that respondents' accused products infringe the Crocs 3D Marks by copying the design features including the size, positioning, number, and shape of holes on the horizontal portion of the upper, the textured strip along the vertical portion with trapezoidal openings, and the textured strip and decorative band on the heel.
points.quote: As shown in Figure 3 below, Cape Robbin and Accused Products bear designs that are likely to cause confusion with the Crocs 3D Marks. In particular, the size, positioning, number, and shape of the holes on the horizontal portion of the upper of the Accused Products is confusingly similar to the 3D Marks.

points.point: Crocs alleges that respondents' accused products are likely to cause confusion with Crocs' trademarks and have already caused actual confusion. Customer reviews on retail websites show consumers referring to accused products as 'Crocs,' such as reviews stating 'I so love my crocs' and 'I love these platform crocs' when purchasing Cape Robbin or Akira products.
points.quote: One such "Verified Buyer" Toya, claims in a January 18, 2021 review that "I so love my crocs": Another "Verified Buyer", Bianca, wrote a review on December 28, 2020 stating, "I love these platform crocs"

points.point: Crocs alleges trademark infringement under Section 32(1) of the Lanham Act, false designation of source/unfair competition under Section 43(a), and dilution under Section 43(c) of the Lanham Act with respect to the Asserted Trademarks.
points.quote: Respondents have also violated Section 337(a)(1)(A) by engaging in unfair methods of competition, false designations of source, and/or likely dilution of one or more trademarks that Crocs uses in connection with the Crocs Shoes.

points.point: Crocs has established a domestic industry with both technical and economic prongs. The technical prong is satisfied by Crocs designing and developing Crocs Shoes in the United States that practice the Asserted Trademarks. Over the past three years, Crocs sold more than 23 million pairs generating $521.4 million in revenue in 2020, more than 12 million pairs generating $248.4 million in 2019, and more than 7.5 million pairs generating $131.8 million in 2018.
points.quote: Over the past three calendar years, for example, Crocs has sold: more than 23 million pairs of Crocs Shoes and generated $521.4 million in revenue in 2020; more than 12 million pairs of Crocs Shoes and generated $248.4 million in revenue in 2019; and more than 7.5 million Crocs Shoes; and generated $131.8 million in revenue in 2018.

points.point: Crocs distributes Crocs Shoes bearing the Asserted Trademarks through major retailers including Nordstrom, Journeys, Foot Locker, Dick's Sporting Goods, REI, and online platforms like Amazon and Zappos, as well as through its own website www.crocs.com and retail stores in multiple countries.
points.quote: Crocs distributes its iconic footwear through a vast network of domestic distribution channels, including major retailers and department stores such as Nordstrom, Journeys, Foot Locker, Finish Line, Urban Outfitters, Shoe Carnival, Designer Shoe Warehouse, and Famous footwear

points.point: To design and develop Crocs Shoes, Crocs makes significant investments in plant and equipment, employs significant labor and capital, and makes substantial investments in the exploitation of the Asserted Trademarks through design and research and development activities.
points.quote: Crocs Shoes sold domestically are designed and developed in the United States. To design and develop the Crocs Shoes, Crocs makes significant investments in plant and equipment, employs significant labor and capital, and makes substantial investments in the exploitation of the Asserted Trademarks through activities such as design and research and development.

points.point: Crocs' Classic Clog was conceptualized as a boat shoe and became recognized by 2005 as a standard-bearer in fashion footwear, professional footwear, and casual lifestyle footwear markets. The shoe's distinctive appearance features holes and textured elements that form the basis of the 3D Marks.
points.quote: Crocs' iconic Classic Clog was conceptualized during a sailing trip and originally presented to consumers as a boat shoe. Soon after, it became apparent that the shoe appealed to consumers of all demographics seeking fun and friendly, comfortable footwear.

points.point: The Crocs 3D Marks are non-functional. They feature one-of-a-kind ornamental design characteristics giving the impression of a fun and distinctively quirky clog-like shoe. The distinctively gentle slope of the upper gives the shoe a unique, recognizable outline, and competitors have virtually infinite non-infringing footwear styles available.
points.quote: They 3D Marks feature one-of-a-kind ornamental design characteristics that give the overall impression of a fun and distinctively quirky clog-like shoe for which Crocs is well-known. The distinctively gentle slope of the upper gives the shoe a unique, recognizable outline.

points.point: The Crocs Word Mark encompasses several standard character marks for 'CROCS' registered for use in footwear and in lightweight, slip-resistant footwear specifically. It was first used in November 2002 and federally registered August 24, 2010, with renewal on October 4, 2019.
points.quote: The Word Mark encompasses several standard character marks for "CROCS", which are registered for use in footwear and in lightweight, slip-resistant footwear specifically. The Word Mark was first used in November 2002.

points.point: Neither the 3D Marks nor the Word Mark were subject to a prior registration or unsuccessful registration, and all registrations are on the Principal Register of the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office.
points.quote: Neither the 3D Marks nor the Word Mark were subject to a prior registration or unsuccessful registration.

points.point: Crocs previously obtained a General Exclusion Order and Cease & Desist Order in ITC Investigation 337-TA-567 regarding foam footwear infringing U.S. Patents 6,993,858 and D517,789. The '789 patent was upheld by the Federal Circuit and is now expired, after which a flood of knockoffs has appeared. Crocs is also involved in ongoing District of Colorado litigation since 2006 involving patent infringement claims.
points.quote: Following the ALJ's initial determination, the Commission issued its decision finding no violation of section 337. Certain Foam Footwear, Inv. 337-TA-567, 73 Fed. Reg. 450, 73-74 (Aug. 1, 2008). However, on remand from a reversal of that decision by the Federal Circuit, the Commission ultimately issued a General Exclusion Order and a Cease & Desist Order to prohibit importation of the infringing footwear.

points.point: Crocs is involved in District of Colorado litigation that has been ongoing since 2006 involving claims of infringement of several patents including the '789 patent, in cases Crocs, Inc. v. Effervescent et al., Case No. 06-cv-00605-PAB-KMT, and U.S.A. Dawgs, Inc. v. Snyder et al., Case No. 16-cv-02004-PAB-KMT (consolidated).
points.quote: Crocs is also involved in litigation in the District of Colorado, which has been ongoing since 2006 and involves claims of infringement of several of Crocs' patents, including the '789 patent. See Crocs, Inc. v. Effervescent et al., Case No. 06-cv-00605-PAB-KMT (D. Colo), U.S.A. Dawgs, Inc. v. Snyder et al., Case No. 16-cv-02004-PAB-KMT (D. Colo.) (consolidated).

points.point: Crocs seeks a General Exclusion Order excluding from entry into the United States all imported shoes that violate Crocs' rights in the Asserted Trademarks due to evidence of likely circumvention of any limited exclusion orders and a pattern of violation.
points.quote: Because Respondents' conduct evidences likely circumvention of any limited exclusion orders that may issue and a pattern of violation, Crocs seeks a General Exclusion Order pursuant to Section 337(d) excluding from entry into the United States all imported shoes that violate Crocs' rights in the Asserted Trademarks.

points.point: Crocs has licensed the Asserted 3D Marks on only one occasion: a 2017 partnership with luxury footwear designer Balenciaga, where cross-over shoes featuring the 3D Marks were sold for $850 at high-end retailers including Barneys New York and sold out during pre-release. Crocs has not licensed the Word Mark.
points.quote: Specifically, in 2017 Crocs unveiled a licensing partnership with famed footwear designer Balenciaga. These shoes retailed for $850, and were described as one of the "hottest trends" of 2018 by Business Insider.

points.point: Since its founding in 2002, Crocs has sold nearly 800 million pairs of shoes in over 90 countries. The company was named 'Brand of the Year' by Footwear News in 2005, launched the largest footwear IPO in history in 2006 raising approximately $208 million, and reported sales of $1 billion worldwide for the first time in 2011.
points.quote: Since the company launched in 2002, Crocs has sold nearly 800 million pairs of shoes in over 90 countries, and garnered widespread recognition of its comfort-driven, revolutionary footwear, making Crocs one of the ten largest non-athletic footwear brands in the world.

points.point: Crocs' trademarks have become famous through widespread publicity. By 2006, the Classic Clog was recognized as 'a global phenomenon.' The design has been featured extensively in media, social media, and through high-profile public figures including President George W. Bush, Prince George, and numerous celebrities.
points.quote: Since its debut, Crocs footwear bearing the Crocs 3D Marks and Crocs Word Mark has received substantial publicity. By 2006, the Classic Clog had already morphed into "a global phenomenon" thanks to its strange look.

points.point: In 2020, Lyst, the largest global fashion search platform, reported that the Classic Clog embodied in the Crocs 3D Marks was the eighth most wanted item in the world. The New York Times declared that 'Crocs Won 2020.' The Classic Clog garnered nearly 25 billion observed media impressions in 2020 alone.
points.quote: In 2020, the largest global fashion search platform, Lyst, reported that, based on web searches, the Classic Clog that is embodied in the Crocs 3D Marks was the eighth most wanted item in the world. The New York Times declared that "Crocs Won 2020," Exhibit 28, and fashion bloggers predicted that "2021 will be the Year of the Croc."

points.point: Crocs has made considerable investments to build the goodwill and widespread recognition embodied in the Asserted Trademarks through design, research and development, and strategic marketing campaigns including the 'Ugly Can Be Beautiful' campaign in 2005 and the 'Come As You Are' campaign in 2013.
points.quote: Building on these measures, the company implemented a return to the basics that relied on the goodwill it had established around the Crocs 3D Marks and Crocs Word Mark over the past decade by reintroducing the Classic Clog with attention-grabbing celebrity partnerships and a fresh ad campaign that acknowledged the company's detractors.

rejected.point: Crocs seeks cease-and-desist orders directing respondents to halt the importation, marketing, advertising, demonstrating, warehousing of inventory for distribution, sale, and use of imported articles in the United States under Section 337(f).
rejected.quote: Crocs further seeks cease-and-desist orders directing Respondents to halt the importation, marketing, advertising, demonstrating, warehousing of inventory for distribution, sale, and use of imported articles in the United States pursuant to section 337(f).
rejected.rejected: quote not found in the filing

rejected.point: Crocs devotes significant time and resources to stopping infringement of its 3D Marks and Word Mark through diverse enforcement actions. Each year, customs officials worldwide seize hundreds of thousands of shoes bearing unauthorized Crocs marks. In 2018, Crocs' defense efforts resulted in termination of over 70,000 online auctions for infringing products and shutdown of over 1,500 websites in the United States alone.
rejected.quote: The scale of this infringement requires constant attention. Each year, customs and other enforcement officials around the world seize hundreds of thousands of shoes that improperly bear the Crocs 3D Marks and/or Word Mark. In more recent years, the rise in consumer online shopping has enabled the sale of infringing footwear on an unprecedented scale. For example, in 2018, Crocs' defense efforts resulted in the termination of over 70,000 online auctions for infringing products, and the shutdown of over 1,500 websites, in the United States alone.
